question: How do prototype methods (K-means, LVQ, Gaussian mixtures) and k-nearest-neighbour classifiers work, when do they succeed, and how can the metric be adapted to fix their high-dimensional bias?

limits: Nearest-neighbour and prototype methods are 'highly unstructured' and 'typically not useful for understanding the nature of the relationship between the features and class outcome' (p.459).
The Cover-Hart bound is asymptotic and assumes zero bias; the authors say 'In real problems the bias can be substantial' (p.468).
With high-dimensional features the bias-variance tradeoff is less favourable for NN regression than for classification (p.459).
LVQ is defined by an algorithm rather than an optimisation criterion, which makes its properties hard to understand (p.462-463).
Authors say they have little practical experience with editing/condensing procedures and found no systematic comparison in the literature (p.481).
Simulation results (Figs 13.2-13.5, 13.15) are single or ten-realization runs without reported numeric tables; the DANN advantage is shown only as boxplots.
Nearest-neighbour is too slow for online use in the ZIP code application; neural nets were built to mimic it (p.475).
practices: Standardize every feature to mean 0 and variance 1 in the training sample before Euclidean distance in prototype and kNN methods (p.459-460, p.465).
Choose k (or prototypes per class R) by an objective data-based method such as cross-validation, because the best value is situation dependent (p.469, citing Fig 13.4 and Ch. 7).
Use small k for low-bias high-variance fits; 1-NN has low bias and high variance, 15-NN gives a much smoother boundary than 1-NN (p.465-466).

When the data have known invariances, build them into the metric (tangent distance) or augment the training set with transformed copies ('hints'); hints work when the invariance space is small, tangent distance when there are many (p.474).

In high dimensions adapt the metric per query (DANN: form a 50-point neighbourhood, estimate W and B, stretch along zero-eigenvalue directions of B*) or reduce dimension globally via eigenvectors of the averaged between-centroid matrix (p.477-480).
Use epsilon=1 in the DANN metric, which 'seems to work well in general' (p.477).
Use the 1-NN error rate as a rough guide to the best achievable error: Bayes error is at least half of the asymptotic 1-NN error (p.468).
To reduce storage, edit/condense the training set (multi-edit, Hart's condensing); use fast neighbour-search algorithms to reduce compute (p.480-481).

For K-means classification, run K-means separately inside each class with R prototypes, label the KxR prototypes, assign a query to the closest prototype; LVQ can start from that solution and move prototypes away from other classes (p.460-462).

terms.definition: Methods that represent the training data by a set of points in feature space, each with a class label; a query is classified to the class of the closest prototype.
Iteratively moves R cluster centres to minimize total within-cluster variance by alternating assignment to nearest centre and recomputing cluster means.
Online algorithm: sample a training point, find the closest prototype; if same class move it toward the point by epsilon*(x_i - m), otherwise away; decrease epsilon toward zero.
Gaussian mixture is soft (responsibilities/weights across clusters), K-means is hard.
Memory-based; find the k training points closest to the query x0 and classify by majority vote, ties broken at random.
Distance taken as the shortest Euclidean distance between any transformed version of the first image and any transformed version of the second.
Approximates each image's invariance manifold by its tangent line and uses the shortest distance between two tangent lines.
Add transformed versions of each training image to the training set and use a standard NN classifier (Abu-Mostafa 1995).

Discriminant adaptive nearest-neighbour: metric at each query point from local within- (W) and between-class (B) covariance of its 50 nearest neighbours; spheres data wrt W then stretches along zero-eigenvalue directions of B*.

code.snippet: mj(k) <- mj(k) + eps (xi - mj(k)) if gi = k (same class); mj(k) <- mj(k) - eps (xi - mj(k)) if gi != k; eps decreased toward 0 each iteration
Bayes error = 1 - p_k*(x); 1-NN error = sum_k p_k(x)(1 - p_k(x)) >= 1 - p_k*(x)
easy: Y = I(X1 > 1/2); difficult: Y = I(sign(prod_{j=1..3}(Xj - 1/2)) > 0)
